lead: This unit explains combustion inside spark-ignition and compression-ignition engines: the stages, the flame, the pressure rise, and the abnormal cases called knock and pre-ignition. After it, you can read a pressure-crank angle trace, calculate delay and pressure-rise rates, and choose a combustion chamber for an SI or CI engine.
about: Unit 3 explains how the fuel-air mixture burns inside SI and CI engines, and why the same pressure rise can be normal in one engine and knocks in another. Chapter 3.1 follows the three SI stages from spark to afterburning. Chapter 3.2 connects flame speed to the rate of pressure rise. Chapters 3.3 and 3.4 separate knock, detonation and pre-ignition, then list the factors that make knock worse. Chapter 3.5 shifts to CI engines: ignition delay, premixed burn, mixing-controlled burn and late burn. Chapter 3.6 uses that delay to explain diesel knock and its control. Chapter 3.7 shows how swirl, squish and tumble mix the charge. Chapter 3.8 applies all of it to SI and CI combustion chamber shapes.

chapters.idea: Combustion in an SI engine is a three-stage process: ignition lag, flame propagation and afterburning.
chapters.depth: Cover the spark-ignition combustion sequence from spark to end of burning. Define ignition lag, flame propagation and afterburning. Explain the flame front as a thin reaction zone moving into unburnt mixture. Relate each stage to crank angle and to the pressure-crank angle trace. Ignition lag is about 0.001 to 0.002 s in a normal engine. Some syllabi call ignition lag the preparation phase. Mention cyclic variation briefly.

figure.aria: Timeline from 15 degrees before top dead centre to 62 degrees after top dead centre: ignition lag ends at 12 degrees after TDC, flame propagation ends at 42 degrees, and afterburning ends at 62 degrees.

chapters.example: A spark fires at 15° bTDC. Ignition lag is 1.5 ms. The engine runs at 3000 rpm. Find the ignition lag in crank degrees and the crank angle where ignition starts. Then mark flame propagation of 30° and afterburning of 20° on a crank-angle timeline.
chapters.trap: Ignition lag ends when pressure starts to rise, not when the flame reaches the cylinder wall. Do not mix lag with flame propagation.
chapters.prereq: Unit 1: four-stroke SI working principle; Unit 2: spark timing.
chapters.leave: Valve timing and ignition hardware to Unit 1 and Unit 2; emission formation to Unit 6.

chapters.idea: Flame speed sets how fast the flame front sweeps the charge, and the mass burning rate sets the rate of pressure rise.
chapters.depth: Define flame velocity as flame travel distance divided by time. Distinguish laminar flame speed from turbulent flame speed. Explain flame front area, unburnt charge density and chamber volume as controls on pressure rise. Show how to read average rate of pressure rise from a pressure-crank angle plot. Mention that fast burn raises peak pressure nearer TDC. Keep chemistry of flame reactions brief.

figure.aria: Line from 10 degrees after TDC at 30 bar to 25 degrees after TDC at 60 bar; its slope is the average rate of pressure rise.

chapters.example: At 10° aTDC the cylinder pressure is 30 bar; at 25° aTDC it is 60 bar. Find the average rate of pressure rise in bar/°CA. At 3000 rpm, convert it to bar/ms.
chapters.trap: A high flame speed alone does not fix the pressure-rise rate. Mass burning rate and chamber volume also matter.
chapters.leave: Detailed ignition timing and spark advance to Unit 2; cycle analysis to Unit 1.

chapters.idea: Knock starts after spark by end-gas autoignition; pre-ignition starts before spark; detonation is severe knock with pressure waves.
chapters.depth: Define normal combustion as flame travel from the spark plug. Define knock as autoignition of end gas after the spark, causing pressure oscillations. Define pre-ignition as ignition before the spark, often from a hot spot. Define detonation as very rapid combustion with supersonic pressure waves, a severe form of knock. Some syllabi call knock 'detonation' loosely; keep the meanings separate. Mention visible symptoms and damage.

figure.aria: Classification tree: abnormal combustion branches into knock after spark and pre-ignition before spark; detonation sits under knock as the severe pressure-wave form.

chapters.example: A petrol engine has spark at 18° bTDC. In case A, pressure oscillations begin at 6° bTDC. In case B, a hot spot ignites the mixture at 22° bTDC. Identify each as knock or pre-ignition. In case C, the pressure wave after knock travels at supersonic speed; name the severe form.
chapters.trap: Knock begins after spark; pre-ignition begins before spark. Detonation is not a separate everyday event in the list; it is severe knock.
chapters.prereq: Chapters 3.1 and 3.2: normal flame travel and pressure rise.
chapters.leave: Knock sensors and ignition control to Unit 2; emission effects to Unit 6.

chapters.idea: Knock depends on fuel, engine design and operating conditions, so changing one factor can make knock better or worse.
chapters.depth: Group factors into fuel, engine and operation. Fuel: octane number and composition. Engine: compression ratio, spark timing, combustion chamber shape, bore and cooling. Operation: speed, load, mixture strength and coolant temperature. Explain direction of each effect. Some syllabi call octane number the anti-knock rating. Keep fuel rating tests brief.

figure.aria: Tree of knock factors under fuel, engine and operation; fuel includes octane number and mixture strength, engine includes compression ratio, spark timing and chamber shape, and operation includes speed, load and coolant temperature.

chapters.example: Classify each change as increasing or decreasing knock tendency: (a) compression ratio 8 to 10, (b) spark advanced from 15° to 25° bTDC, (c) coolant temperature 80°C to 95°C, (d) octane number 91 to 95.
chapters.trap: A higher octane number reduces knock; a higher compression ratio or more spark advance increases knock. More is not always worse.
chapters.leave: Fuel octane testing and additives to Unit 2; turbocharging effects to Unit 4.

chapters.idea: CI combustion has four stages: ignition delay, premixed burn, mixing-controlled burn and late burning.
chapters.depth: Start with the heterogeneous charge: fuel is injected into hot air, so mixture formation and ignition overlap. Define ignition delay as start of injection to first pressure rise. Explain premixed burn from fuel accumulated during delay, then mixing-controlled burn, then late burn. List factors affecting delay: cetane number, air temperature and pressure, injection timing, injection pressure, engine speed and load, atomization. Some syllabi call delay the ignition delay period.

figure.aria: Timeline from 12 degrees before TDC: ignition delay ends at 2.4 degrees after TDC, premixed burn ends at 10.4 degrees, mixing-controlled burn ends at 40.4 degrees, and late burning ends at 55.4 degrees.

chapters.example: Injection starts at 12° bTDC. Ignition delay is 1.2 ms at 2000 rpm. Find the delay in crank degrees and the crank angle where ignition starts. Premixed burn lasts 8° and mixing-controlled burn lasts 30°. Find the end of mixing-controlled burn; take late burning as 15°.
chapters.trap: Delay period is measured from start of injection to first pressure rise, not from TDC and not from spark.
chapters.prereq: Unit 1: CI working principle; Unit 2: injection timing and nozzles.
chapters.leave: Injection pump and CRDI hardware to Unit 2; spray penetration details to Unit 2.

chapters.idea: Diesel knock comes from a long ignition delay that lets fuel accumulate and then burn too fast in the premixed phase.
chapters.depth: Only a few universities teach this topic; keep it short. Define diesel knock as harsh combustion noise from a rapid premixed burn after long delay. Explain the chain: long delay, fuel accumulation, rapid premixed burn, high pressure rise, knock. Control methods: higher cetane number, retarded injection, warmer intake air, pilot injection, better atomization, chamber design. Do not confuse it with SI spark knock.

figure.aria: Flow from long ignition delay to fuel accumulation, rapid premixed burn, high pressure rise and diesel knock; a cetane booster shortens the delay.

chapters.example: A diesel engine runs at 1500 rpm. Ignition delay is 1.4 ms. Find the delay in crank degrees. Raising cetane number from 45 to 50 cuts delay to 1.0 ms. Find the reduction in crank degrees.
chapters.trap: Diesel knock is not spark knock. It is caused by long ignition delay and too much premixed fuel.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 3.5: CI stages and delay period.
chapters.leave: Injection system types and nozzle design to Unit 2; advanced low-temperature combustion to Unit 6.

chapters.idea: Swirl, squish and tumble are organised air motions that mix fuel and air and shorten combustion.
chapters.depth: Define swirl as rotation about the cylinder axis, squish as radial inward flow as the piston nears TDC, and tumble as rotation about a diameter. Define swirl ratio as swirl speed divided by engine speed; it has no units. Explain how each motion helps mixture formation in CI engines and flame speed in SI engines. Mention turbulence briefly. Some syllabi call squish 'squish flow'.

figure.aria: Tree of air motion: swirl about the cylinder axis with swirl ratio, squish as radial flow at TDC, and tumble about a diameter.

chapters.example: An engine runs at 2000 rpm. Swirl ratio is 2.2. Find swirl speed in rpm. The squish clearance is 2 mm and squish velocity is 10 m/s. Find the time to move 2 mm.
chapters.trap: Swirl ratio is swirl speed divided by engine speed and has no units. Squish is radial flow at TDC, not a swirl.
chapters.prereq: Unit 1: engine components; Chapter 3.5: CI mixture formation.
chapters.leave: Turbocharging and variable geometry to Unit 4; optical flow measurement to Unit 6.

chapters.idea: A combustion chamber must mix the charge, burn it quickly and avoid hot spots, so SI and CI engines use different shapes.
chapters.depth: Cover design objectives: high turbulence, short flame travel, no hot spots, good breathing, easy starting and low heat loss. SI chambers: wedge, hemispherical and bathtub. CI chambers: direct injection with a bowl in the piston, and indirect injection with a prechamber. Explain factors influencing chamber design: bore, compression ratio, valve size, injection location and cooling. Some syllabi call indirect injection 'IDI'.

figure.aria: Tree of combustion chambers: SI types are wedge, hemispherical and bathtub; CI types are direct injection with a piston bowl and indirect injection with a prechamber.

chapters.example: A CI engine has bore 100 mm and stroke 110 mm. Its direct-injection bowl is 55 mm diameter and 18 mm deep. Clearance volume is 70 cm³. Estimate bowl volume as a cylinder and express it as a percentage of clearance volume.
chapters.trap: Direct-injection diesel has the bowl in the piston; indirect injection uses a prechamber. Do not label a prechamber engine as direct injection.
chapters.prereq: Chapters 3.1 to 3.7: SI stages, knock, CI stages, delay and air motion.
chapters.leave: Advanced HCCI, RCCI and low-temperature combustion to Unit 6; cooling and supercharging to Unit 4.
